messages:
noah: Quick follow-up from the authn/authz RFC — can we sketch the tradeoffs of decoupling service authorization from project/org scoping?
elaine: High level: decoupling simplifies per-service policies but complicates tenant isolation unless we enforce a binding layer.
ravi: Agree. If we separate, we need a clear binding contract: service_id -> allowed_project_ids. Otherwise lateral access risk.
noah: Right. Two patterns I see: 1) brokered binding (a central broker issues scoped credentials for services per-project) 2) attribute-based runtime checks (service asserts attributes and request path is checked against policy).
maya: Brokered binding pros: explicit audit trail, easier to revoke per-project access. Cons: extra hop, stateful broker, migr pain.
elaine: Attribute-based pros: stateless, simpler runtime. Cons: harder to prove intent, more fragile to token forging if signing not strict.
ops-bot: Deploy note: adding broker will touch authz-api, token-issuer, and ops pipelines. Recommend canary in staging with 2 services.
ravi: Migration idea: start by making broker optional. Services continue to use current keys; broker can mint short-lived project-scoped tokens for calls that need cross-project access. Gradual enforcement via header flag.
maya: Implementation sketch:
```
# pseudo
POST /broker/mint { service_id, project_id, scope }
-> { scoped_token: "ey...", expires_at: 167... }
```
Service uses scoped_token for downstream requests.
elaine: Important: tokens must be audience-bound and have embedded project claim and sig. No wildcard projects. Also bind to originating service_id.
noah: Observability ask: we need per-token lineage so we can answer "which service and which project caused this eval". Broker should emit event with mint_reason.
ravi: Policy evaluation cost: adding broker reduces chance of runtime expensive policy lookups (precomputed allow lists), but introduces latency once at mint time. We can cache minted tokens at service for short TTL to avoid hammering.
maya: Edge-case: background jobs that fan-out to many projects. Broker could mint a multi-project token but prefer per-project tokens to keep blast radius small. If too many projects, use batch calls via ephemeral worker that runs with elevated project ACLs and strong audit.
elaine: Backwards compat: introduce a header X-Authz-Mode: "legacy|scoped|required" so we can rollout. Start with legacy->scoped (opt-in) then scheduled flip.
noah: Security review points: rotation UX, broker availability (SLOs), key compromise blast radius, replay protection. Add jti + nonce and short TTLs.
ravi: Ops checklist: 1) broker HA (multi-AZ) 2) metrics: mint_rate, mint_errors, token-use-latency 3) rollout plan doc + migration runbook.
maya: UX for devs: SDK helpers to mint and cache tokens transparently. Example snippet in SDK to fallback to legacy key if broker unavailable (with warning).
elaine: Policy model note: keep project-level RBAC (role -> project resource) but allow additional service-scoped role bindings. Avoid adding a new role grammar if possible.
noah: Can we enumerate high-level migration milestones?
ravi: Milestones: 1) design + security review 2) broker prototype + SDK helper 3) internal canary (2 non-critical services) 4) staged opt-in rollout + metrics 5) require scoped tokens for cross-project endpoints 6) deprecate legacy long-lived project keys.
maya: Also add: create a small eval suite with prompts/endpoints that validate authz decisions end-to-end for both patterns.
noah: Sounds good. I'll draft a short RFC follow-up with the broker-first path and the opt-in headers. Include the migration milestones and the ops checklist.
elaine: +1. Add a section on incident playbook: broker outage -> fallback policy -> revoke window -> expedite rotation.
ravi: I'll volunteer to prototype the mint endpoint and tests.
maya: I'll draft the SDK helper and the rollout doc.
noah: Thanks all. tagging this for the next auth sync. :thumbsup:
